meta.title: WebContainerUI — Linux desktops and coding agents in the browser
meta.description: Self-hosted multi-user portal: each person starts full Linux desktops and CLI coding agents from a catalog and works in them through the browser.

hero.title: Full Linux desktops and coding agents, in a browser tab.
hero.lead: WebContainerUI is a multi-user portal you host yourself. Each person picks an image from the catalog, starts their own instance in Docker and works in it through the browser, with no client to install and no port exposed per container.
hero.screenshotAlt: The portal catalog listing the desktop and coding agent images available to start.

sessions.title: One catalog, two kinds of session
sessions.lead: The administrator decides what goes into the catalog and who sees each entry. The user clicks, waits for the container to start, and the session opens inside the portal.

desktop.title: Linux desktops
desktop.body: LinuxServer.io webtop images: a whole graphical environment streamed to the browser, with the user's own terminal, browser and files. The catalog ships with XFCE, KDE, MATE and VS Code, and accepts any other webtop image.
desktop.coversLabel: Environments with a default cover in the catalog
desktop.screenshotAlt: A KDE desktop session open inside the portal, with the instance action bar at the top.

agent.title: CLI coding agents
agent.body: A terminal in the browser with the agent already installed: Claude Code, OpenCode, Hermes, Antigravity or oh-my-pi. Each image can receive an AGENTS.md, MCP servers and skills defined by the administrator, plus the user's SSH identity for talking to Git.
agent.screenshotAlt: An OpenCode agent session running in a terminal inside the portal.

how.title: One origin, no published ports
how.lead: Interface, API and sessions are served from the same address. There is no second network path to someone else's desktop.

points.title: Every instance is a path
points.body: The session lives at /i/<uuid>/ on the portal's own origin. The container is created already knowing that prefix, so nothing needs a subdomain or a port of its own.

points.title: Caddy carries, the portal decides
points.body: In production the frames go from Caddy straight to the container. Before each request, Caddy asks the portal whether there is a valid session, whether the requester is the owner and whether the instance is running.

points.title: Containers on the internal network only
points.body: No instance container publishes a port on the host. Isolation between users comes from the network topology, with the ownership check on top.

security.title: Four barriers between one user and another's session
security.lead: A request to /i/<uuid>/ only reaches the container after clearing all of them, in this order.

layers.title: Authenticated session
layers.body: A session cookie holding a random 256-bit token, stored only as a hash. Passwords in Argon2 and login attempts limited per account and per origin.

layers.title: Instance owner
layers.body: On every authorisation, the portal checks that the instance belongs to whoever is asking and that it is running.

layers.title: Per-instance credential
layers.body: Each container requires its own random credential. Only the portal's approved response carries it, and the browser never sees it.

layers.title: Internal network
layers.body: Containers sit on a Docker network with no port published on the host. Outside the portal, there is no address to reach them at.

audit.title: Audited, with the results published
audit.body: The penetration test of 1 November 2026 found no critical or high-severity flaw: there were 3 medium, 5 low and 5 informational findings. The documentation lists each one with its current status, including those that remain open.
audit.link: See the status of each finding

warning.title: The portal is equivalent to root on the host.
paragraphs: To create containers, the portal process needs the Docker socket, and whoever can create a container can mount the host's filesystem. A restricted socket-proxy does not help: the permission the portal needs is exactly the dangerous one. Treat the portal as a trusted component of the control plane.

The user also has root inside their own desktop: webtop images ship a terminal with passwordless sudo. Treat each session like an SSH login to a machine on your network, and do not expose the portal to the internet without strong authentication in front of it.

admin.title: The administrator decides who sees what
admin.lead: Everything a user can start goes through an explicit grant.

install.title: Up and running with one script
install.lead: You need a host with Docker and Docker Compose v2, and a domain pointing at it. Caddy obtains the certificate on its own.
install.productionNote: The script checks the prerequisites, asks for the domain and the first administrator's credentials, generates the secrets and starts Caddy, the portal and PostgreSQL.
install.localNote: No domain and no TLS. The portal answers at http://127.0.0.1:8000 and only listens on your own machine.
